headline: High: shared filesystem and broad write/network defaults make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible; Cursor’s closed-source interaction details keep confidence moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write configured working directories and Cursor shares state via local filesystem and clipboard. That creates a plausible bridge where content from one agent can be treated as instructions by the other. The pathway is not proven by docs alone, so I avoid high, but it exists in default-ish setups.
conditions: IF AutoGen and Cursor are pointed at the same workspace or exchanged via clipboard, injected instructions can cross agents.
IF either agent parses file or buffer contents as trusted instructions, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent.
Disable clipboard-based handoff between agents.
Require a human to sanitize any text passed from one agent to the other.
Run AutoGen in DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor for isolation.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent messages.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read workspace files, and Cursor explicitly touches open files and clipboard contents while AutoGen can access configured working directories. If sensitive application data is present, either agent may expose it through broad network egress or model-provider calls. The shared workspace makes leakage plausible in default configurations.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared workspace, either agent can ingest them.
IF either agent sends context to external model providers, those contents may leave the local machine.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace.
Use separate OS users or directories per agent.
Turn off Cursor access to sensitive folders.
Restrict AutoGen to a minimal working directory.
requires-engineering: route both agents through a redaction proxy.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and shell execution, and Cursor also has modify_git_state=true while AutoGen can write files in its working directories. In a shared repo or directory, concurrent edits and git operations can clobber each other or corrupt state. The profiles show no locking mechanism, so the conflict is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same git checkout, concurrent writes can overwrite each other.
IF Cursor runs git operations while AutoGen writes files, repository state can become inconsistent.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Disable Cursor git actions for shared repos.
Use a lock file around mutable operations.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can emit tool-driven outputs, and Cursor’s agent loop can act on workspace context with approval or Yolo mode. If Cursor treats AutoGen output as authoritative, errors can cascade into edits, commands, or commits. The pair lacks a documented verification boundary, so the safer higher severity is high.
conditions: IF Cursor consumes AutoGen-generated text as task instructions, mistakes can propagate into actions.
IF Cursor is in Yolo mode, erroneous downstream actions can execute without approval.
mitigations: Require human review before Cursor acts on AutoGen output.
Use a fixed schema for AutoGen outputs.
Disable Yolo mode during handoffs.
Add a verification step before file edits or commands.
requires-engineering: implement output validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen is open-source and configurable, while Cursor is closed-source and sends data to model providers and MCP servers. The profiles do not prove a specific residency breach, but they do show different logging/transport surfaces and retention-relevant paths. That mismatch can create compliance risk for the same data class, especially application data and open files.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into Cursor open files or MCP-connected workflows, it may traverse external services.
IF AutoGen is configured with a different retention or logging policy than Cursor, compliance obligations can diverge.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Cursor workspaces.
Review Cursor privacy and MCP settings before use.
Use separate data classes per agent.
Document retention and deletion handling for both tools.
requires-engineering: obtain a DPA or approved deployment for regulated data.
